paragraphs.heading: Physics for the sky
paragraphs.text: Celestial mechanics is the branch of astronomy that studies how objects in space move and how they pull on each other through gravity. It applies classical mechanics to bodies such as stars and planets to produce ephemeris data. Its modern analytic form began with Isaac Newton's Principia in 1687, though Newton wanted the field called rational mechanics. Pierre-Simon Laplace brought in the name celestial mechanics more than a century after Newton.

paragraphs.heading: Kepler joins causes to predictions
paragraphs.text: Before Johannes Kepler, predicting exactly where planets would be had little to do with debates about what made them move. Kepler tied the two together, combining the geometrical astronomy used from Ptolemy to Copernicus with physical ideas in a work of 1609. Using his physical principles and Tycho Brahe's observations, he worked out laws of planetary orbits. His elliptical model made predictions of planetary motion far more accurate, years before Newton's law of gravitation.

paragraphs.heading: Newton's one set of laws
paragraphs.text: Isaac Newton is credited with the idea that the same physical laws describe planets, the Sun and the Moon as well as cannonballs and falling apples. In that way he united motion in the heavens with motion on the ground. Using his law of gravity, he derived Kepler's laws for elliptical orbits from the gravitational two-body problem. For two bodies pulling on each other, Newtonian mechanics gives a set of orbital elements that predicts their future positions with reasonable accuracy.

paragraphs.heading: The three-body problem
paragraphs.text: Add a third body and the problem can no longer be solved exactly, so perturbation theory is used to find an approximate answer. In 1762 Leonhard Euler gave the first periodic solution: three balance points on a straight line through the two main masses, where a body of tiny mass would stay in a stable orbit. In 1772 Joseph-Louis Lagrange found two more stable orbits, at the corners of equilateral triangles made with the two main masses. Together these became known as the Lagrange points.

paragraphs.heading: From Lagrange to chaos
paragraphs.text: Lagrange also reworked classical mechanics to put more weight on energy than on force, with one equation in polar coordinates able to describe any orbit, even parabolic and hyperbolic ones. That helps with planets and comets, and more recently with spacecraft paths. Later, Henri Poincaré proved the three-body problem to be non-integrable. In other words, its general solution cannot be written out using algebraic and transcendental functions of the bodies' coordinates and velocities. One of his ideas later became the basis of chaos theory.

paragraphs.heading: Mercury's puzzle
paragraphs.text: Careful calculation also turned up puzzles. In 1849 Urbain Le Verrier reported that Mercury's perihelion, its closest approach to the Sun, moves forward by 43″ every century. The known gravitational tugs, worked out with Newton's law, could not explain this shift. Le Verrier later put it down to a proposed planet orbiting inside Mercury's orbit.
